metadata.title: Three Witnesses to Two Per Second
metadata.subtitle: three fields, one number, one missing qualifier
metadata.presenter: Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI
metadata.builder_note: Structure is TESTIMONIAL: three independent witnesses agree on one number, each cross-examined with the same three questions, and the third narrows its testimony. Deliberately not Week 21's concentric shape. See BEATS-DRAFT.md.
metadata.source_note: Source is an auto-converted Substack essay, not a produced video: slug and content title disagree, recap sits at beat 2, no FACTCHECK. Narration here is original; nothing is inherited from the source beat sheet.

beats.narration_text: Two per second. A room of people tapping a finger at whatever speed feels natural. A stranger walking down a street, measured through the top of their head. The stressed syllables in an English sentence. Three measurements, three fields that do not cite each other, and the same number.

legibility.artifact: Three spectra stacked, drawn one per sentence: tap intervals, head acceleration, speech envelope. Each carries its own citation line beneath it, legible as that measurement is named - van Noorden & Moelants (1999); MacDougall & Moore (2005); He et al. (2024). A single vertical rule at 2 Hz lands across all three on the last line and holds. No branding, no title, no logo anywhere in this beat.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: This is Tanmay Kulkarni in for Humanitarians AI. That number gets used to argue that human beings run on one shared internal clock. I went and read the three studies underneath it. Two of them hold. The third one never said what it gets quoted as saying.

legibility.artifact: Title card: Three Witnesses to Two Per Second. Presenter line beneath.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: So here is the test I am going to run, and you can run it on anything. Three questions. What exactly was measured. How many people. And what qualifier sits in the original sentence that falls off when the finding gets retold. I am not asking all three of every witness. Each one gets the question that breaks the version you have heard, and there is a rule for choosing. Reach for question one when the number is suspiciously round. Question two when the result is surprising. Question three when a finding has travelled a long way from the field that produced it.

legibility.artifact: The three questions written as a numbered card, built one line at a time as each is spoken, each paired with its selection trigger: round number, surprising result, travelled far. This card persists as a corner reference for the rest of the film; the question in play and its trigger light up whenever a witness is cross-examined.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Witness one. Music. Ask people to tap at whatever rate feels comfortable, and van Noorden and Moelants modelled the result as a resonance. A system with a natural frequency of two hertz. One tap every five hundred milliseconds. Run large collections of music through that model and the curve peaks near a hundred and twenty beats per minute.

legibility.artifact: Resonance curve drawn live, peak annotated at 120 BPM / 2 Hz. Citation legible on screen for the full beat: van Noorden & Moelants (1999).

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Question one. What exactly was measured. The answer is a peak in a distribution, not a person. Moelants put preferred tapping between a hundred and twenty and a hundred and thirty. A later study measured twenty three people. The average came out at a hundred and four beats per minute, and the range ran from fifty four to a hundred and seventy. The peak is real. Almost nobody sits on it.

legibility.artifact: Question one lights up on the corner card. Same resonance curve, now with the individual measurements scattered over it: n=23, mean 104.6, range 54-170 drawn as points spanning most of the axis. Both citations held side by side at the moment of comparison: Moelants (2002) and Hine et al. (2022).

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Witness two, and a different instrument entirely. MacDougall and Moore fixed accelerometers to the heads of twenty people and recorded ten hours of an ordinary day. Walking, running, cycling, sitting at a desk, riding a bus.

legibility.artifact: Method diagram: head-mounted sensor, a 10-hour timeline banded by activity type. Citation legible: MacDougall & Moore (2005), J Appl Physiol 99:1164-1173.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: What they found, in their words, was a highly tuned resonant frequency of human locomotion at two hertz. Standard deviation, zero point one three hertz. With no evidence of correlation with gender, age, height, weight, or body mass index. Two steps per second. A hundred and twenty steps a minute.

legibility.artifact: Frequency spectrum with the 2 Hz peak and its error band drawn to scale. The quoted phrase appears on screen inside quotation marks with the citation beneath it while it is spoken.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: And it is not one lab. That same paper points back to a laboratory study from more than forty years earlier, which had put preferred step frequency at one point nine five hertz. Different decade, different method, the same answer. Though note what I just did. I am citing that older figure through the newer paper, not from the original.

legibility.artifact: Two values side by side, held: 2.00 Hz (2005, field) and 1.95 Hz (1964, laboratory), with both error bands overlapping. The 1964 value is drawn with a visible dashed link through the 2005 paper, marking it as a second-hand citation.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Question one again. What was measured is where the body resonates, not how people amble. In a study of seventy six adults, a hundred steps a minute counts as moderate exertion, three metabolic equivalents. A hundred and twenty steps a minute is about five. Each extra ten steps a minute adds roughly one. The resonance is real. Everyone strolling at a hundred and twenty all day is not.

legibility.artifact: Question one lights up again. Cadence-to-effort ladder: 100/3, 110/4, 120/5, 130/6, with 120 marked against the 2 Hz rule from the previous beat so the resonance and the effort cost are legible in the same frame. Citation: Tudor-Locke et al. (2019), CADENCE-adults.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: One more piece of honesty, and it is the authors' own. The measurement is solid. The explanation is not settled. They reason from vestibular reflexes and then use the word speculate. Measured result, proposed cause. Keep those apart.

legibility.artifact: The authors' own sentence on screen with the word 'speculate' highlighted in place, citation beneath.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Witness three. Speech carries a nested rhythm. Syllables run in the theta range, roughly four to eight hertz, and the sources disagree inside that window. Underneath the syllables, the stress beat runs at about half that rate. Two hertz.

legibility.artifact: Nested rhythm diagram: syllable band drawn as a range, not a point, with both disagreeing source ranges labelled (4-5 Hz and 5-8 Hz) and cited separately. Stress beat at 2 Hz beneath.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Question three. What qualifier sits in the original. I am going to show you two sentences. Here is the one in the research. The rhythm of the stress foot in English is centred around two hertz. And here is how it usually comes back to you. Speech runs on a two hertz beat. One of those says less than the other. Find it before I say it.

legibility.artifact: Both sentences on screen together, full width, source above and retelling below, with the citation under the source. After the narration ends the frame holds in silence for 2 s with no highlight, no arrow and no motion - the viewer is finding it. This is the only silent hold in the film.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: In English. Two words. They are sitting in the source, and they are gone from the retelling. And with them goes the difference between a fact about people and a fact about a language.

legibility.artifact: The two words isolate and hold in the source sentence; the same position in the retelling below stays visibly empty. Both remain on screen together.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Somebody went and checked. Thirty four listeners. Seventeen native English speakers, seventeen native Mandarin speakers, listening to speech built at stress rates of one, two, and three hertz. Brain to speech tracking peaked at two hertz for the English speakers. For the Mandarin speakers, that peak was absent.

legibility.artifact: Two tracking curves plotted on one axis, English and Mandarin, with the 2 Hz point marked on both. Drawn simultaneously, not sequentially, and held. Citation: He, Buder & Bidelman (2024), Brain and Language 256:105463.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Question two. How many people. Thirty four, with a single channel of recording, and the authors calling their own reading somewhat speculative. So this is not proof that speech rhythm is arbitrary. It is one good study saying the two hertz beat belongs to a language, not to the species.

legibility.artifact: Question two lights up on the corner card. The study's own stated caveats listed verbatim, citation beneath.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: So. Three findings, and all three of them are real. The tapping resonance is real, with far more spread between people than the headline admits. The locomotion result is the strongest of the three. Two methods, four decades apart, agreeing. Though the reason for it is still a hypothesis. And the speech rhythm is real too. It simply was never the universal claim. It said in English the whole time. Nothing here was invented. The story just got wider each time it was passed on, two words at a time.

legibility.artifact: The three-question card returns as three rows, one per witness, each carrying the question that tested it and the scope that survived. The speech leg is narrowed in place by its verdict tag reading 'narrower' against the other two reading 'holds' - built as annotation rather than as a redrawn 2 Hz rule, which would have put a second visual device on an already-full verdict frame.

build.note: animated 4K clip, timed from measured narration

beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it is a measurement, not a search. Tap a finger for thirty seconds at whatever feels natural, and count them. If you land at ninety, or a hundred and forty, you have not broken the model. You have found the spread that one number hides. Then take any claim that separate fields independently agree on something, go to the original sentence, and look for the qualifier. Three Witnesses to Two Per Second. Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI, signing off.

legibility.artifact: A thirty-second counter runs on screen while the instruction is spoken, so the viewer can start immediately. The observed spread is shown as a strip beside it - 54 to 170 with 90 and 140 marked, the two numbers the narration names - rather than re-staging the full witness-one scatter, which would repeat a frame the viewer already read.
